artifacts.synopsis: The SJC sustained Psiaki’s complaint and held that the CPC Session erred by ordaining and installing officers elected at a February 5, 2023 congregational meeting where the congregation’s bylaw excluded communing members under 18 from voting. Reading BCO 6-4, 25-1, and 25-7 together, the SJC ruled that all communing members are entitled to vote and that local bylaws cannot impose an age restriction; the “good and regular standing” language addresses censure, not age. The decision did not annul the completed ordination/installation, but required future elections and installations to comply with the Constitution.

artifacts.synopsis: Members challenged a voting restriction imposed at a congregational meeting. The SJC dismissed the complaint as judicially out of order because BCO 43-1 permits complaints against acts or decisions of church courts, and a congregation is not such a court. It identified other possible routes through a report to Presbytery or review of church records. The adopted decision did not decide whether the voting restriction was constitutionally valid.

artifacts.synopsis: A member challenged Presbytery’s approval of a congregational motion supplementing an assistant-pastor fund, alleging that Session had ceded its budget authority. The SJC denied both issues. The motion addressed a special circumstance, not approval of the budget, and left the salary figure to the elders and deacons; Session had already approved the budget and retained control of church funds. The ruling was confined to the congregation’s particular circumstances and did not approve congregational budget adoption.

4. The Northside Presbyterian Church Session acted out of accord with BCO 25-7 in proposing a revision of church bylaws.

4. The Session did not violate BCO 25-7 by indicating in its plan that the church's bylaws would be revised. A local church may, and often does, have bylaws. Such bylaws are envisioned, not prohibited, by BCO (see
BCO 25-7). There is no indication in the record that the Session intended to alter the PCA's BCO, or that the church's own bylaws would be out of accord with the BCO.

artifacts.synopsis: Complainants challenged a Session plan under which most elders voluntarily resigned, the Session granted severance and benefits to its former pastor, proposed about a year with an interim pastor before a permanent call, and contemplated revising local bylaws. The SJC denied all four items. It held that the BCO permitted jointly considered voluntary resignations, that severance concerned resignation and the budget rather than a pastoral call, and that the plan and bylaw proposal were not themselves unconstitutional. Any later call still had to follow the BCO without undue delay, and local bylaws had to remain consistent with it.
